title: B.C.'s major party leaders to debate tonight ahead of provincial election

image.caption: From left: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby, B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan during the campaign. (CBC News)

items: The only live leaders' debate before British Columbia's provincial election is set to take place tonight in Vancouver at 6:15 p.m. PT.
The debate will include NDP Leader David Eby, B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan.
OneBC's Dallas Brodie and CentreBC's Elenore Sturko are not involved, having agreed to the criteria for a party leader to qualify for the debate in advance.
The debate comes 10 days before voters head to the polls on Oct. 24. You can livestream the event in the video above or on YouTube.

blocks.text: B.C.'s provincial party leaders take the debate stage tonight
The leaders of British Columbia's main political parties will take the stage together tonight for the only live, streamed and televised debate of the provincial election campaign.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby and B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan will debate a wide range of issues important to British Columbians, with less than two weeks to go until voters head to the polls.
How to follow the debate on CBC:

items: Online: Live streaming at the top of this page and on the CBC British Columbia YouTube channel.
On TV: Live on CBC Television (check your TV service provider for channel details).
Listen: Live on CBC Radio One (88.1 FM in Vancouver, 90.5 FM in Victoria, 88.9 FM in Kelowna and 91.5 FM in Prince George).

blocks.text: As of late September, health care, the economy, housing prices and affordability were essentially tied as the "most important" election issues, according to a Leger survey of 1,003 British Columbians over a four-day period.
Taxes and Trump — key focuses for the Conservative and NDP campaigns, respectively — were of lesser importance to Leger respondents.
A separate Angus Reid poll of 801 British Columbians identified cost of living as the top election concern last month, far ahead of health care, the economy and affordable housing.

Eby called the election in September, two years early, saying the province needs a fresh government to adequately respond to the trade conflict between Canada and the United States. Both his political opponents and members of the public have criticized the decision to send voters to the polls just a week after municipal elections this Saturday.
Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute, will moderate tonight's leaders' debate.

items: October 15Eby under pressure to change narrative tonightJustin McElroyEby at a campaign stop in September. (Nav Rahi/CBC)I'm a political reporter with CBC British Columbia. I'll be watching tonight's debate and providing analysis and fact-checking what the party leaders say — and of the three, nobody needs a big night more than the NDP's Eby.Whatever polling advantages Eby had during Kerry-Lynne Findlay's dysfunctional reign as Conservative leader seemed to evaporate as soon as he called a snap election two days after she resigned and was replaced by Doerkson. Attacks on U.S. President Donald Trump, raising questions about whether the B.C. Conservative Party would remove Doerkson as leader, new health-care promises and populist attacks on big gas and grocery companies haven't appeared to move the needle for the NDP, which has trailed in every poll released in the past two weeks. With just 10 days until the election, Eby will be hoping for a couple of moments that change the conversation around the campaign.

Conservatives, NDP running same number of candidatesTom SummerCandidates finalized across 93 ridings in lead-up to B.C. snap electionThe list of candidates for the 2026 B.C. election has been finalized. The Conservatives have a full slate across all 93 ridings, while the NDP is one short at 92. Experts say the smaller parties are likely to play a big role this time around.There are a total of 355 hopefuls in the running to either become an MLA or keep their seat as one. Most of them represent one of 10 political parties, with a handful running as independents or unaffiliated candidates.The Conservatives initially fielded 93 candidates in the race, covering all of the province's ridings, but recently dropped its candidate in Victoria-Beacon Hill after offensive social media posts were brought to light. The NDP is also at 92 candidates, having no representative running in Peace River North. Hamish Telford, a political science associate professor at the University of the Fraser Valley, said the Conservatives have accomplished "quite a feat" running candidates in almost every riding, "considering the turmoil" the party weathered in recent months."It's going to come down to how the smaller parties do in particular ridings," Telford said of the Conservatives and NDP running the same number of candidates.The Greens have 73 candidates in the running, while CentreBC and OneBC have 35 and 33, respectively. Since there are 93 seats in the B.C. Legislature, a party needs to win 47 to form a majority government.

How to catch up on the recent craziness in B.C. politicsAndrew KurjataA man rides a bicycle through Vancouver. (Ben Nelms/CBC)If you haven't been paying close attention to B.C. politics recently, you might find yourself confused by the political news in the past few weeks. Voters are faced with new leaders, new parties and new decisions to make about who should lead the province when they head to the polls.You can find a brief timeline to get you up to date here.

Leaders for CentreBC and OneBC will not be at tonight's debateRhianna SchmunkSturko, left, and Brodie, right. (CBC/The Canadian Press)CentreBC's Elenore Sturko and OneBC's Dallas Brodie are not involved in the leaders' debate. The broadcast consortium, including CBC, Global and CTV, said the criteria for a party leader to qualify for the debate was agreed upon by all its members, but it did not respond to a request for more details. Sturko became leader of CentreBC last month, describing the party as fiscally responsible and socially progressive. She said she wants to appeal to centrist voters who feel they don't have a political home with the NDP or the Conservatives.OneBC formed last year shortly after the Conservatives came within a hair of winning the 2024 provincial election. Brodie, the party's interim leader, is running for re-election in Vancouver-Quilchena.Neither party is running enough candidates to form a majority government.
